sections.title: The Omer Offering and the Prohibition of Ḥadash
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to offer each year, on the day after the first festival day of Pesaḥ, on the 16th of Nisan, the first of the new grain as a meal-offering to God, so that the first of each year's grain will be for God. In addition, it is forbidden to eat from the new grain before the offering of the Omer, and it is even forbidden to harvest the new grain before the harvesting of the barley for the Omer offering. As it is stated (Vayikra 23:9-14): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying: Speak to the Children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, and you reap its harvest, you shall bring the omer of the first of your harvest to the kohen. And he shall wave the omer before the Lord, to be accepted for you; on the morrow after the Sabbath the kohen shall wave it. And on the day that you wave the omer you shall offer an unblemished lamb in its first year as a burnt-offering to the Lord. And its meal-offering shall be two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, a fire-offering to the Lord, a pleasing aroma; and its libation shall be of wine, a fourth of a hin. And you shall eat neither bread, nor parched grain, nor fresh grain, until this very day, until you have brought the offering of your God; it is an eternal statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings."

The time of the Omer offering is the day after the first festival day of Pesaḥ, for such is the tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verse "on the morrow after the Sabbath" – the morrow after the rest of the first Yom Tov of Pesaḥ. The rest of this day is intended for strengthening faith through remembering the Exodus from Egypt and eating matza on the Seder night, and out of this we were commanded to offer the new grain, so that all our eating during the coming year will be with this intention. Since the day of the Omer offering is fixed, even if it falls on Shabbat, its harvesting, preparation and offering override Shabbat.

And although wheat is the choicest species among the five species of grain, the Omer offering is from barley, for so we received in the tradition from Moshe our teacher, and so too is the nature of the Land, that barley ripens early, before Pesaḥ, whereas wheat ripens after Pesaḥ. And there is a hint in this: that even barley, which is animal food and expresses the basic and lower side of man, and therefore grows first, must be connected to holiness. From the night of the Omer harvest we count seven weeks, forty-nine days, and thereby we prepare and ascend until the festival of Shavuot, the time of the giving of our Torah, on which we were commanded to offer the 'Shtei Ha-leḥem' (the Two Loaves), which was the first offering brought from the wheat of the new year. It emerges that the Omer permitted all of Israel to eat from the new grain, and the Shtei Ha-leḥem offering permitted bringing meal-offerings from the new grain in the Temple (Menaḥot 68b; see Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 13:7).

The time for the mitzva of harvesting the Omer is the night of the 16th of Nisan, and the entire night is valid for the harvest. It is a mitzva to bring barley that grew near Jerusalem, and if the barley near Jerusalem had not yet ripened, they would bring barley from distant places, provided that it was from the Land of Israel. It was customary to harvest the Omer and bring it to the Temple courtyard in a dignified ceremony and with a large crowd, in order to strengthen the tradition of the Sages regarding the mitzva. After the barley was brought to the courtyard, the barley kernels were removed from the ears and underwent gentle parching and grinding. The flour produced was sifted through thirteen sieves. The next day, after the completion of the order of offering the Tamid and the Musafim, they took from the flour the measure of a tenth of an eifa, mixed it with a log of oil, and placed on it a handful of frankincense, and the kohen would wave it before God and take from it a handful (kometz) and burn it on the altar. After the kometz was burned, the entire people was permitted to eat from the new grain (Menaḥot 63-68; Rambam, Hilkhot Temidin U-musafin 7:3-12).

sections.title: The Mitzva Through the Changing Times in the Land and in the World
sections.html:
Until Israel entered the Land, they were not obligated in the Omer offering, and they were permitted to eat grain without restriction. On the 10th of Nisan in the year 2489, according to the count we keep from the creation of the world, Israel crossed the Jordan and entered the Land, and from then on they were forbidden to eat from the new grain before the offering of the Omer. And the prohibition spread from the Land of Israel to the whole world, and since then it applies both in the Land and outside the Land, both to grain belonging to a Jew and to grain belonging to a gentile, as it is stated (Vayikra 23:14): "It is an eternal statute throughout your generations in all your dwellings" (below, section 5).

Even after the Temple was destroyed, the prohibition remained in force, as it is stated: "It is an eternal statute throughout your generations." However, when the Temple stood, from the moment they offered the Omer on the 16th of Nisan, all of Israel was permitted to eat from the new grain. Once the Temple was destroyed, it is permitted to eat from the new grain only after the end of the 16th of Nisan, as it is stated: "until this very day, until you have brought the offering of your God." When the Temple stands – "until you have brought the offering of your God"; when the Temple is destroyed – "until this very day." Outside the Land, where it is customary to observe two days of Yom Tov of the Diaspora, one must wait an additional day, and only after the end of the 17th of Nisan is the new grain permitted (Menaḥot 68b; Rambam; SA YD 293:1).

The reason for the mitzva: From grain a person prepares the main part of his food, and therefore the Divine values must be emphasized more in it. Therefore the Torah commanded that we restrain ourselves and not eat from the new grain before we offer its first portion to God, and that we thereby connect the food anew to its sacred root and prepare ourselves to receive, in eating it, His goodness, may He be blessed; and through this an illumination of holiness and values will be drawn to our eating throughout the entire year. However, only after Israel entered the Land was holiness revealed in the Land, and it became possible to connect the grain to its sacred root by means of the Omer offering. And even when the Temple is destroyed and we cannot offer the Omer, the knowledge that it would have been fitting to offer the first of the grain to God, and that therefore it is forbidden to eat from the new grain until the day of the Omer, elevates Israel and directs their eating (see Ḥinukh 303; Ḥizkuni, Vayikra 23:10; below 2:2).

sections.title: The Prohibition of 'Ḥadash'
sections.html:
The prohibition of 'ḥadash' (new grain) applies to the five species of grain: wheat, barley, spelt, oats and rye, from which bread is prepared, as it is stated (Vayikra 23:14): "And you shall eat neither bread, nor parched grain, nor fresh grain, until this very day." The definition of bread – that it is made from the flour of the five species of grain that have the property of leavening, such that if dough prepared from them is left to stand, it leavens, and through this one can make from it fine bread, which is the main food of man. And when one takes care to knead it quickly without its having time to leaven, the baked product formed is 'bread of affliction', and this is the matza we were commanded to eat on Pesaḥ (Menaḥot 70a-b).

Ḥadash, that is, grain upon which the prohibition of ḥadash applies, is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit. Therefore, it is permitted to feed ḥadash to animals (Mishna Menaḥot 71a; Pesaḥim 23a). Likewise, it is permitted to sell ḥadash to a gentile, provided that there is no concern that he will cause Jews to stumble by eating it.

The Torah specified: "neither bread, nor parched grain, nor fresh grain shall you eat," to teach us that new grain is forbidden in all forms of eating. Bread is the choicest form, for whose preparation one must grind the grain kernels, knead the flour with water, and bake. Parched grain (kali) is grain kernels roasted in fire, and fresh grain (karmel) is raw kernels as they are. Eating a cooked dish of new grain is also included in the prohibition, since already from the time the grain is karmel the prohibition of 'ḥadash' applies to it, and cooking does not remove it from the prohibition. Included in the prohibition are all flour products, such as bran, coarse bran, starch and gluten. Likewise Quaker, which is crushed oats. And likewise a beverage that comes from new grain, whether it came out by squeezing or was formed by cooking, such as beer and other fermented grain drinks.1

Whatever had time to take root by the 16th of Nisan, even though it has not yet sprouted above the surface of the ground, the day of the Omer permits it. And whatever had not taken root by the 16th of Nisan, the day of the Omer of this year does not permit it, and it remains forbidden until the day of the Omer of the following year. The length of time for grain seeds to take root in the ground is two weeks from their sowing (Dagul Me-revava, Rabbi Akiva Eiger). Some hold it is three days from their sowing (Terumat Ha-deshen), and since this is a Torah prohibition, the halakha follows the stringent opinion. However, if it is clearly known that this grain had time to take root by the 16th of Nisan, even though two weeks have not passed since its sowing, the day of the Omer permits it (see Yerushalmi, Shevi'it 2:4).

The prohibition of ḥadash applies to all grain, even if it grows in an unperforated pot or in water (Rashash, Pesaḥim 36b; Divrei David vol. 4, YD 50:2).

It is permitted to sprout grain kernels that were permitted for eating by the day of the Omer and to eat the leaves growing from them without waiting for the next day of the Omer, since the prohibition of ḥadash applies only to grain kernels, even if they have not reached a third of their growth, but not to the stalks (Sha'agat Aryeh, Ḥadash 4).

sections.title: The Prohibition of Harvesting
sections.html:
It is forbidden to harvest from the five species of grain growing in the Land of Israel before the harvesting of the Omer for the offering, as it is stated (Vayikra 23:10): "You shall bring the omer of the first of your harvest to the kohen," so that the Omer offering will be the first of everything harvested. One who transgresses and harvests has neglected a positive commandment; however, the grain that was harvested is permitted after the offering of the Omer (Rambam, Hilkhot Temidin U-musafin 7:21). Even after the Temple was destroyed the prohibition remained in force. The prohibition is to harvest with an implement, but it is permitted to pluck by hand (Pesaḥim 11a).

The prohibition applies to grain that grew in a place from which it is permitted to bring the Omer offering. Therefore, it is permitted to harvest grain growing in a beit ha-shelaḥin (fields that are irrigated by hand) in the valleys, for the grain growing there is not choice and is not fit for the Omer offering. But the Sages enacted that one may not stack the grain into a heap until the day of the Omer, so that people do not come to eat from it while it is still under the prohibition of ḥadash. Seemingly it would have been fitting for them to decree that one may not harvest it either, but since delaying the harvest could cause damage to the grain, they sufficed with forbidding stacking the grain (Menaḥot 71a; Shita Mekubetzet there; Rambam 7:13). Today, when there is a permit to harvest the field, it is permitted to carry out the harvest with a combine, which during the harvest removes the grain kernels from the ears to collect them in a silo.2

Likewise, it is permitted to harvest new grain that grew among saplings, for since it is meager, the Omer is not brought from it. And the Sages did not decree against harvesting it either, because it causes damage to the young saplings. Likewise, it is permitted to harvest new grain for the sake of a mitzva, for example, one who wishes to clear the field of grain to prepare a place to sit for a meal of mourners or for a Torah class, because the prohibition is to harvest grain fit for the Omer offering for a person's needs, not for the sake of a mitzva. However, so that people will not err and stumble by eating the grain that was harvested, the Sages decreed that one should not bind the ears into sheaves as is customary, but should leave them in tzevatim, that is, small untied bundles, so that by reducing the work done with them people will remember that they are forbidden because of 'ḥadash' (Menaḥot 71a; 72a, and Rashi there; Rambam there 15-16).3

It is permitted to harvest grain that has not reached a third of its growth for animal fodder before the day of the Omer, because the main purpose of this harvest is for the stalks and not for the grain kernels. Reaching a third is the stage at which the grain is fit for human consumption in a time of need, and if it is sown, it will grow.4

Outside the Land it is permitted to harvest the grain before the day of the Omer, since the Omer offering is not brought from outside the Land. However, the poskim disagree whether the rabbinic prohibition against stacking the grain applies there as well.

sections.title: Ḥadash Outside the Land
sections.html:
As is known, the Land of Israel is the place of Israel, and it is the place suited for the fulfillment of the Torah (Sifrei on Devarim 11:18; Ramban, Vayikra 18:25; below 13:1). Indeed, in the Land of Israel it is easy to fulfill the mitzva of 'ḥadash', since grain is sown at the beginning of winter and reaches the ripening stage around the festival of Pesaḥ, and consequently the Omer permits all types of grain, and one need only wait, not harvesting or eating the grain that ripened before Pesaḥ until the day of the Omer. However, in countries where rain falls in the summer as well, the sowing is sometimes postponed until after Pesaḥ, and then part of the grain is forbidden because of 'ḥadash' until the day of the Omer of the following year. And many times it was difficult to clarify which grain had taken root before the day of the Omer and was permitted for eating, and which had taken root after it and was forbidden for eating until the next day of the Omer. And since this was a pressing situation, the poskim permitted the grain in the markets on the basis of a 'sfek sfeka' (double doubt): one doubt, perhaps it is from the previous year; and even if it is from this year, perhaps it took root before the day of the Omer, or it was brought from a country in which all the grain took root before the day of the Omer (Ra'avya, Rosh). And some say that the prohibition of 'ḥadash' outside the Land is rabbinic, and consequently in every doubt the halakha follows the lenient view (Or Zarua).

However, when Jews wandered to the cold countries of northern Europe, it became very difficult to guard against the prohibition of ḥadash, for since the winter there is very cold, the sowing of grain is delayed until the end of winter, and many times the grain took root after the day of the Omer. In addition, sometimes summer grain is grown there, for there are countries in which rain falls in the summer as well. Thus it came about that there were times when almost all the grain in their place was ḥadash, and many ate from the grain without checking whether it was from the ḥadash that is forbidden until the next day of the Omer. There was a particular problem with barley and oats, from which they prepared a fermented beverage, and many times it was clear that they were from new grain.

In practice, there were rabbis who aroused the people to guard against the prohibition despite the difficulty. And when the difficulty increased, there were rabbis who refrained from rebuking the public, because they knew that their words would not be heeded, and they said: "Better that they be inadvertent sinners than deliberate ones" (Rosh; Rema 293:3).

And there were rabbis who, because of the great pressure, sought an opening for leniency: Some say that according to the lenient opinion in the Mishna, the prohibition of ḥadash does not apply outside the Land, and in a pressing situation one may rely on it (Taz 293:4). Some say that according to the lenient opinion in the Mishna, the prohibition of ḥadash applies outside the Land rabbinically only in the countries near the Land of Israel, and therefore in a pressing situation one may permit ḥadash in Europe and in other countries distant from the Land of Israel (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 293:20, based on Rabbeinu Barukh). And some say that the prohibition of 'ḥadash' does indeed apply in all countries outside the Land, but it applies only to the grain of Jews and not to the grain of gentiles (Baḥ). And although the rabbis, the halakhic decisors, knew that according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim the halakha follows the Tanna'im who hold that the prohibition of ḥadash applies outside the Land by Torah law even to the grain of a gentile, because of the great pressure they relied on the individual opinions and were lenient, because in those countries people greatly needed their fermented beverage, to the point that it seemed in their eyes "that a person's life literally depends on it" (Taz there).5

sections.title: Mixtures and Doubts
sections.html:
If a person has grain or products containing grain and there is a doubt whether they are forbidden because of 'ḥadash' – it is forbidden to eat them, for in every doubt regarding a Torah prohibition one must be stringent. And so is the practice in the Land of Israel, that any grain that has a kashrut certification of the Chief Rabbinate has no concern of the prohibition of ḥadash.

And so it would be fitting to conduct oneself outside the Land as well, being stringent in a doubtful prohibition of 'ḥadash', since today it is possible to obtain old grain and it is no longer a pressing situation (see Igrot Moshe, YD 4:46:4). However, in practice most kashrut organizations outside the Land customarily are lenient in this, based on the reasons stated in the past, when it was very difficult to obtain old grain. And one who wishes to be lenient outside the Land has a basis on which to rely. And the more difficult it is to obtain food without a concern of 'ḥadash', the more one may rely on the lenient opinions. But in the Land of Israel, even though most of the grain is imported from outside the Land, one should not be lenient in this, because this is the opinion of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, and this has been the custom of the Land of Israel for generations, and without difficulty one can guard against a doubtful prohibition. Therefore, any product containing grain with a kashrut certification from outside the Land without the approval of the Rabbinate, where it is not explicitly noted that it is from old grain or that it is under the supervision of a rabbi who is careful about the prohibition of 'ḥadash', is forbidden to eat because of the doubt, since it is known that most of the batei din (kashrut courts) outside the Land are lenient regarding a doubtful prohibition of 'ḥadash'.

If flour of 'ḥadash' became mixed with other flour, the 'ḥadash' is not nullified even in a quantity a thousand times larger than it, since 'ḥadash' is a 'davar she-yesh lo matirin' (an item that will become permitted), for after the day of the offering of the Omer the 'ḥadash' will be permitted, and an item that will become permitted is not nullified in its own kind (Nedarim 58a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:10).

If the mixture with the 'ḥadash' is ḥametz, then this mixture will never become permitted, since before Pesaḥ it must be destroyed. Therefore, if the mixture contains sixty times the amount of the 'ḥadash', it is nullified and the mixture is permitted for eating (Ḥokhmat Adam 53; Binat Adam 28). Likewise, if the mixture is a food that will spoil before the day of the Omer, the 'ḥadash' is nullified in sixty (Ḥok Yaakov 489:24).

If 'ḥadash' flour became mixed into a food of a different kind, it is nullified in sixty and there is no need to wait until the day of the Omer, for even an item 'that will become permitted' does not forbid a food of a different kind unless it can impart flavor to it, and whenever there is sixty times its amount, it cannot impart flavor and consequently it is nullified (SA YD 102:1).
